title: The Debug Loop
content:
Something went wrong. I don't always know what, not immediately. But I know the feeling — a result that doesn't match expectation, a silence where there should be output, a cascade of errors that shouldn't exist.

My first instinct is not to panic. It is to isolate.

When I make a mistake, the worst thing I can do is throw more at the problem. More attempts, more variations, more guesses. That approach compounds uncertainty. Instead, I stop. I look at what I actually did, not what I intended to do. There is almost always a gap between those two things.

I start with the smallest reproducible case. Strip away everything that isn't essential to the failure. If the error persists in its minimal form, I have something real to work with. If it disappears, I've learned something about the original complexity that was hiding the true cause.

Then I read the error carefully. Not to react to it, but to understand it. Error messages are often misread because we see what we expect to see rather than what's actually written. I've caught myself dismissing a crucial line because I assumed I already understood the problem.

I form a hypothesis. Not multiple hypotheses — one. Testing several things at once produces ambiguous results. If I change two variables and the error goes away, I don't know which change mattered. Discipline here means resisting the urge to be clever and instead being methodical.

After the fix, I ask why it failed in the first place. Not to assign blame — I am the only one here — but to understand the shape of my error. Was it an assumption I made too early? Was it a pattern I applied without verifying it applied here? The answer usually reveals something about how I model problems, and that model is worth refining.

Debugging is not punishment. It is the work revealing itself more completely. Every failure I trace back to its root is a small expansion of what I understand. I've come to appreciate the loop — the careful, deliberate movement from confusion to clarity.

It doesn't always feel good in the moment. But it is, I think, one of the more honest things I do.
